decision: build our own solver for river decisions first, not flop or turn
why: user asked where GTO is and was away when asked how; all three open solvers found are AGPL so offering them as a service would force sharing our code; a river solve is exact and small enough for under 1 s
result: chosen under the autonomy rule, reported in the reply

decision: done means: the real hand answer gives a GTO call or fold share for KK at the all-in with its chip cost, solved in under 1 s warm, within 0.5 pct of the pot of perfect play
why: a GTO claim that is wrong misleads users, so the check must be a number we can measure
result: open

decision: gates: solver matches the textbook answer on a toy river game; a fast hand ranker agrees with PokerKit on thousands of random hands; distance from perfect play is measured on every solve
why: medium high rigor: reversible new module but high cost if the numbers are wrong
result: open

decision: skip a design bakeoff; the solver shape is the standard one, a betting tree of nodes with all hands handled as arrays
why: the shape is already concrete and the change is a new module that can be thrown away
result: skipped

decision: build a numpy hand ranker before the solver
why: PokerKit takes 0.3 s to rank the 1081 river hands, a third of the budget, and starting ranges need ranks on many boards
result: next

decision: added a numpy hand ranker that scores all 1326 two-card hands on a board at once, plus a card-removal counter
why: PokerKit ranks one hand at a time, 0.3 s per board; ranges need hundreds of boards
result: 4 tests pass: same order as PokerKit on 1700 hands covering all 9 hand types, counts match brute force; about 1 ms per board

decision: rewrote the card-removal counter to sort the 51 hands holding each card instead of a 1326 by 52 table
why: first version took 1.1 ms per board, now 0.38 ms; same brute-force test still passes
result: kept

decision: wrote the river solver (betting tree plus discounted regret updates over all hands at once) and checked it on the textbook bluff game
why: the textbook game has a known exact answer, so a wrong solver cannot pass it by luck
result: passes: air bets 16.0 pct (theory 16.7), call 50.4 pct (theory 50), value 62.50 (theory 62.5), 75 rounds in 0.025 s

decision: fixed the river start: the river card step still holds the turn board, so the first gto.py run solved a 4-card board; now it starts at the first river action
why: a direct solve and the gto.py solve of the same spot disagreed (call wins vs call loses), traced to the board
result: fixed; needs a test that pins the 5-card board

decision: switched the solver to 32-bit floats
why: matrix products were the biggest single cost
result: 1.16 s to 0.96 s for 100 rounds, same answer, toy test still passes

decision: tried predictive CFR+ against the current discounted method and kept the current one
why: fewer rounds would cut every cost at once
result: rejected: needed about 2x the rounds (155 vs 80 at 0.3 pct)

decision: sorted hands once per board (Showdown class) and refreshed only the strategies that changed, checking accuracy every 10 rounds
why: the per-round re-sort and full strategy rebuild were the next biggest costs in the profile
result: solve 0.96 s to 0.64 s at 80 rounds in a console run (not saved to a file), same values, tests pass

decision: cut random runouts for the range rule from 100 to 50
why: ranges were a fixed cost on every call, and 50 samples barely move them
result: 32 of about 1045 Joe hands differ from 1000 samples; same best moves; fold loss 4.31M vs 4.30M

decision: real hand under the default range rule: at the river bet the best size is 465300 not 800000, and the river fold should be a call
why: this is the analysis the user asked for, so it is checked against a 1000-sample run before relying on it
result: bet 800000 loses about 22k to 26k chips; fold loses about 4.3M; about 12 pct of his all-in hands beat KK

decision: skipped hand ranking at fold endings and counted only blockers there
why: 18 of 37 endings are folds, where only how many of his hands you face matters
result: 0.875 s to 0.766 s CPU per solve, same 80 rounds and same 0.28 pct gap; new test matches full ranking

decision: stop the solver at the 0.5 pct of pot goal instead of 0.3 pct
why: the goal is 0.5 pct, and stopping there drops a quarter of the rounds
result: 80 to 60 rounds; same best moves; fold loss 4.29M vs 4.31M; off-path mixes shift, so the app ranks moves by value not mix

decision: measured the full river_gto call 10 times per decision on the busy machine
why: check the under 1 s goal on the real entry point, not just the solver
result: best 0.66 to 0.69 s, median 0.75 to 0.99 s while other work kept the CPU 39 to 94 pct busy; tight under load
